question: When a minimal causal transformer policy is trained with PPO to sort fixed-length permutations through adjacent swaps, does increasing its embedding width improve an interpretable internal rank representation and gap-based action heuristic after task accuracy has saturated?

key_findings.claim: The study trains 475 minimal transformer actor-critics on a finite adjacent-swap sorting environment while varying embedding dimension from 2 to 128.
key_findings.evidence: Inputs are permutations of distinct tokens at lengths 6 or 8. A decoder-only model with learned token and position embeddings, one causal single-head attention block, a linear layer, and actor/critic heads chooses an adjacent transposition. PPO receives +1 only when a swap finishes sorting and -0.001 otherwise, with a 1,000-step episode cap and 1M, 2M, or 10M total timesteps. The appendix provides PPO settings but not the complete allocation of agents to widths, horizons, layers, and seeds.

key_findings.claim: Small embeddings are often sufficient for same-length task success, especially at sequence length 6, whereas length 8 remains substantially harder.
key_findings.evidence: For dimensions above 16, 99.2% of length-6 agents but only 37.4% of length-8 agents reportedly attain 100% action accuracy. Table 1 averages are 96.7% at 1M and 95.5% at 10M for length 6, and 74.3% at 2M and 90.7% at 10M for length 8. Accuracy is defined by enumerating all permutations and checking whether the policy chooses an adjacent inversion, an action that reduces inversion count and therefore lies on a shortest adjacent-swap path.

key_findings.claim: Among near-perfect agents, wider embeddings correlate with a more monotonic final-row attention score ordering after accuracy has largely saturated.
key_findings.evidence: The Kendall-like non-inversion proportion between token values and the last attention row rises with width and levels near dimension 30. The reported plateau is about 87% for length 6 and 78% for high-accuracy length 8; low-accuracy length-8 agents average 57%, near the 50% random-order reference. Because Figure 2 excludes non-near-perfect agents, especially most length-8 runs, the plot supports a conditional association within selected successful policies, not an unconditional width effect.

key_findings.claim: The adjacent-gap heuristic is a useful partial predictor of actions, but it is not a complete recovered circuit.
key_findings.evidence: For high-accuracy agents, the chosen action matches the top-ranked adjacent score gap only 76.2% at length 6 and 76.8% at length 8; allowing either of the top two gaps raises this to 94.0% and 92.5%. Low-accuracy length-8 agents reach only 54.1% top-2. No weight-level derivation, intervention, ablation, activation patch, or counterfactual manipulation establishes that the value matrix and output layer causally calculate these differences. Figure 4 gives only r-squared = 0.56 between two descriptive metrics.

key_findings.claim: The displayed attention equation is inconsistent with the quantities analyzed later.
key_findings.evidence: Section 3.3 defines the 'attention weights' as W = QK^T/sqrt(d_k), omitting softmax. Raw scaled dot products are neither restricted to [0,1] nor normalized, yet Section 5 says each last-row value lies between 0 and 1, and the appendix visualizes them as attention weights. Either the formula omitted softmax or the later analysis silently switches from logits to probabilities; the paper never resolves which matrix its metrics use.

key_findings.claim: Increasing embedding dimension is confounded with increasing model size, optimization geometry, and the probability of successful training.
key_findings.evidence: Embedding dimension is also the query/key dimension and the hidden width feeding attention, values, embeddings, and the actor/critic heads, so changing it changes many parameter matrices and total parameter count. There is no parameter-matched control, isolated Q/K-rank intervention, fixed-parameter wider bottleneck, or alternative architecture. Length-8 success itself changes sharply with width, and the representation plots condition on success. The data therefore do not identify embedding dimension per se as the cause of a stronger representation.

key_findings.claim: The label 'world model' is not operationalized by a predictive or causal world-model test.
key_findings.evidence: The model is never asked to predict next permutations, transitions, rewards, or hidden environment variables; it emits one action from a fully observed fixed permutation. The analyzed code may be a learned scalar ranking of token identities sufficient for action selection. Moreover, the final causal-attention row is architecturally the only row that can see the entire prefix, so state-relevant information is expected there. Calling this a minimalist world model is an interpretation, not a result distinguished from a static rank feature or policy representation.

key_findings.claim: The proposed 'local greedy trap' contradicts the mathematics of adjacent-swap sorting.
key_findings.evidence: Section 5.4 says a model can be trapped by swapping an obviously incorrect local pair because resolving a larger global inversion may require temporarily increasing local inversions. For a permutation, however, swapping any adjacent inverted pair reduces the global inversion count by exactly one, and the minimum number of adjacent swaps equals that count. Repeated local inverted-pair swaps are therefore always optimal; bubble sort requires no temporary increase. A failing agent may choose a non-inverted pair or fail to locate an inversion, but that is not the described greedy trap.

key_findings.claim: The sign and ranking definition of the purported decision rule changes across the paper.
key_findings.evidence: Observation 2 first says the chosen transposition is the 'largest difference'; Section 5.3 says the most positive or most negative difference; Section 5.5 says choosing the most negative difference guarantees a correct swap. Metric 3 says differences are sorted but does not define sign, absolute value, direction, or ties, and calls top-2 one of n predictions even though a length-n sequence has n-1 adjacent actions. These variants are not equivalent, so the claimed circuit is underspecified.

key_findings.claim: The inference from monotonic attention scores to an orderly token embedding geometry is not established.
key_findings.evidence: Section 6.1 calls monotonicity a direct consequence of key vectors arranged consistently in embedding space. But each score is a dot product with an input-dependent final-token query plus learned positional components; monotonic scores for observed permutations do not imply that keys or token embeddings lie along one global direction. The paper provides violin plots of scores, not key/query decompositions, probes, or interventions that remove position and final-token effects.

key_findings.claim: The experiments test exhaustive interpolation at two fixed lengths, not generalization or robustness.
key_findings.evidence: Policies are trained on random states from the same 720- or 40,320-permutation spaces on which all possible initial permutations are later evaluated. There is no held-out length, vocabulary extrapolation, noisy token, partial observation, perturbation, pruning, or cross-task transfer experiment. Claims in the discussion about longer-sequence transfer, noise robustness, policy brittleness, or downstream benefit are explicitly future possibilities rather than measured results.

key_findings.claim: The aggregate study is underreported relative to its claim of hundreds of robust experiments.
key_findings.evidence: The paper states 475 agents and multiple seeds but never lists the exact dimension grid, number of seeds per cell, training-horizon allocation, one-versus-two-layer allocation, randomization protocol, stopping/selection criteria, or regression specification. Table 1 even has missing length/horizon cells and a lower mean for length-6 10M than 1M. Figures show means and 95% intervals but do not define whether intervals are across agents, seeds, or fitted means. No code or artifact URL appears in the paper despite the abstract's release statement.

key_findings.claim: The paper appropriately limits its architectural and domain scope, but even one cited implementation detail is editorially unreliable.
key_findings.evidence: The limitations restrict conclusions to adjacent transpositions, lengths 6/8, and shallow single-head transformers, with compute preventing broader sequence lengths. In Methods, however, the sentence attributing PPO's stability and parallelizability cites reference [7], which is a 2025 knowledge-graph convolution paper; PPO is reference [20]. This does not change the experiment but reinforces that the implementation narrative needs a reproducible artifact.

method.core_idea: Use a tiny causally masked transformer as a PPO policy for repeated adjacent swaps, sweep its embedding/hidden width, and measure whether successful wider agents encode token rank monotonically in the final attention row and choose swaps associated with large neighboring score gaps.
method.mechanism: A permutation of tokens 1 through length is embedded with learned token and position vectors. A single-head causal self-attention block produces a final hidden representation for actor and critic heads. PPO learns from a sparse terminal +1 reward and -0.001 step cost. Evaluation exhaustively queries all permutations at length 6 or 8, reports whether the action swaps an adjacent inversion, compares the ordering of token values with final-row attention scores by normalized non-inversions, and ranks the chosen action among adjacent attention-score differences.
assumptions: A scalar ordering visible in one attention row qualifies as a faithful internal world model rather than a policy feature or static token-rank code.
The analyzed W is consistently defined even though the displayed equation omits softmax and later values are treated as normalized probabilities.
Changing embedding dimension while also changing hidden width, Q/K/V dimensions, parameter count, and optimization geometry isolates representational capacity.
Conditioning representation analyses on near-perfect accuracy does not create width-dependent selection bias.
The undisclosed distribution of 475 agents across dimensions, training horizons, layers, and seeds is sufficiently balanced for the confidence bands.
The final row is informative because of an emergent algorithm rather than simply because causal masking makes it the only row that can attend to the full sequence.
High rank correlation of attention scores with token values implies a coherent global key/embedding geometry despite query and positional dependence.
Top-1/top-2 descriptive action agreement and cross-metric correlation are enough to identify the value/output computation without a causal test.
Performance on all states from the same fixed-length finite environment is evidence relevant to robustness and world-model quality.
A terminal sorting reward plus small step penalty reliably selects shortest-path policies rather than reward-equivalent idiosyncratic behavior.
The intended adjacent-gap statistic has a fixed sign, magnitude, and tie convention despite inconsistent prose definitions.
One or two shallow layers and one head adequately model the capacity effect of wider modern transformers.

techniques.role: Turns sorting into a finite fully observed control problem whose valid progress actions are adjacent inversions.
Uses learned token/position embeddings and one single-head attention block so the final row can be inspected.
Learns swap actions from a terminal sorting reward and per-step penalty without demonstration labels.
Varies the hidden/query/key dimension from 2 to 128 across 475 reported agents.
Evaluates the learned first action on every permutation at a fixed sequence length.
Measures rank agreement between token numerical order and scores in the final attention row.
Measures whether the selected swap corresponds to one of the largest neighboring attention-score differences.
Plots internal metrics mainly for near-perfect agents, excluding many unsuccessful length-8 runs.
Shows the empirical distribution of final-row scores associated with each token identity for selected agents.

evaluations.setting: 475 PPO agents across embedding dimensions 2-128 and permutation lengths 6 and 8 (pp. 4-6).
evaluations.metric: Fraction of all fixed-length permutations for which the chosen adjacent swap is an inversion-reducing action.
evaluations.result: Above dimension 16, 99.2% of length-6 agents and 37.4% of length-8 agents reach 100%; Table 1 reports mean accuracy up to 96.7% and 90.7% for the two lengths.
evaluations.baseline: No non-transformer, supervised, fixed-embedding, parameter-matched, or exact-algorithm baseline; comparisons are only among widths, lengths, and partly reported training horizons.

evaluations.setting: Near-perfect length-6 and length-8 agents across embedding width (pp. 5-6).
evaluations.metric: Normalized proportion of non-inversions between token values and the last attention row.
evaluations.result: The mean rises with width and plateaus around dimension 30 at about 87% for length 6 and 78% for successful length 8; unsuccessful length-8 agents average 57%.
evaluations.baseline: A 50% random-order reference. Conditioning on success removes most length-8 agents and is not corrected in the width analysis.

evaluations.metric: Share of chosen actions matching the top one or top two ranked adjacent attention-score gaps.
evaluations.result: Top-1 is 76.2%/76.8% and top-2 is 94.0%/92.5% for length 6/8; low-accuracy length-8 agents have 54.1% top-2.
evaluations.baseline: No alternative heuristic, learned probe, chance top-k calculation, or causal ablation; the sign/absolute-gap definition is inconsistent across sections.

evaluations.setting: All agents in the cross-metric scatter (p. 8).
evaluations.metric: Linear association between top-1 gap agreement and non-inversion proportion.
evaluations.result: Figure 4 reports r-squared = 0.56 with a fitted line and 95% interval.
evaluations.baseline: A descriptive bivariate regression with no control for embedding width, sequence length, accuracy, seed, or training horizon.

evaluations.setting: Selected attention visualizations for a fully ordered permutation and two high-accuracy agents (pp. 12-14).
evaluations.metric: Heatmap and violin-plot monotonicity of final-row attention values by token identity.
evaluations.result: One selected agent has a perfectly ordered row for one ordered input; both selected agents have monotonic mean token scores, with broader distributions for the agent with more inversions.
evaluations.baseline: Qualitative selected cases only; no position/query decomposition, alternative layer/head, or intervention on the purported rank direction.

evaluations.setting: One example successful length-6 training run (pp. 12 and 14).
evaluations.metric: PPO clipped value loss over global steps.
evaluations.result: Figure 8 shows the selected successful run's value loss approaching zero.
evaluations.baseline: No matched unsuccessful run, policy loss, entropy, return curve, width comparison, or seed distribution despite text speculating that failed runs would not stabilize.

limitations: Author-stated: only adjacent transposition sorting and sequence lengths 6 and 8 are studied.
Author-stated: architectures are shallow, single-head transformers; deeper and multi-head models are not explored.
Author-stated: compute limits broader lengths and training runs, so the result is evidence of a trend rather than an exhaustive characterization.
Reviewer-identified: embedding dimension changes total capacity and many parameter matrices at once, with no parameter-matched or Q/K-only control.
Reviewer-identified: the exact distribution of 475 agents across widths, horizons, layer counts, and seeds is missing.
Reviewer-identified: the attention formula omits softmax although later metrics assume values in [0,1].
Reviewer-identified: the adjacent-gap sign, magnitude, tie handling, and even number of candidate actions are underspecified.
Reviewer-identified: representation plots postselect high-accuracy agents, especially excluding most length-8 runs, and can confound width with successful optimization.
Reviewer-identified: no causal intervention or weight-level derivation validates either proposed mechanism.
Reviewer-identified: the task is fully observed and fixed length; the policy never predicts dynamics, so 'world model' is not operationally distinguished from a rank feature.
Reviewer-identified: evaluating all states in the same finite spaces used during random-state training is interpolation, not length or distribution generalization.
Reviewer-identified: no robustness test introduces noise, partial observability, token remapping, pruning, quantization, or adversarial states.
Reviewer-identified: no MLP, RNN, noncausal transformer, fixed embedding, supervised learner, or hand-coded heuristic baseline tests architectural specificity.
Reviewer-identified: learned position embeddings and the input-dependent final query are not separated from token-rank effects.
Reviewer-identified: top-1 gap agreement near 76% and non-inversion plateaus below 90% leave substantial behavior unexplained.
Reviewer-identified: means and 95% intervals are not accompanied by sample counts per point, interval construction, hypothesis tests, or a controlled regression.
Reviewer-identified: the abstract says metrics and analyses are released, but the paper supplies no artifact URL or complete configuration table.
Reviewer-identified: the local-greedy failure explanation is mathematically wrong for adjacent-inversion swaps.
Reviewer-identified: one PPO implementation claim cites an unrelated knowledge-graph paper instead of the PPO reference.
failure_modes: Low-width or unsuccessfully optimized agents may encode only noisy local token differences and choose non-inverted pairs.
Length-8 PPO frequently fails to reach a perfect policy even above dimension 16, so width does not guarantee convergence.
A monotonic attention row can be a noncausal correlate: deleting or rotating it may leave the actual action circuit intact.
The purported top-gap rule mispredicts roughly 23-24% of high-accuracy actions at top-1 and still misses 6-7.5% at top-2.
Postselecting successful policies can make wider models appear representationally cleaner simply because wider models optimize more often.
Changing the final token or positional embeddings can alter the final query and attention ordering without changing token identity ranks.
A policy memorizing all 720 length-6 states can score perfectly without learning a length-general sorting algorithm.
The policy can fail immediately on length 7, 9, repeated values, unseen tokens, arbitrary swaps, or noisy observations because none is trained or tested.
Sparse terminal rewards and a 1,000-step cap can create unstable or seed-sensitive PPO training, especially in the 40,320-state length-8 space.
If W denotes raw logits rather than softmax weights, the reported [0,1] score analyses and visual interpretation are applied to a different quantity than Equation 3.3 defines.
An absolute largest gap may select a correctly ordered pair, while the most negative signed gap selects an inversion; ambiguity in sign can change every action prediction.
A static scalar token-rank code may not transfer when token labels are permuted or values are presented compositionally rather than as fixed identities.
Increasing width can improve optimization while making internal computation less identifiable in richer multi-head/deep architectures, the opposite of the paper's extrapolation.
reusable_insights: Mechanistic metrics can continue changing after behavioral accuracy saturates, so capacity studies should measure internal geometry as well as outputs.
For adjacent-swap sorting, inversion count gives an exact potential function and a ground-truth criterion for every action, enabling exhaustive mechanistic audits.
Rank correlation between an internal scalar and a known latent variable is a useful hypothesis generator but should be followed by interventions and weight algebra.
Capacity sweeps need parameter-matched controls and an explicit separation between representational width and probability of successful optimization.
When only successful runs are analyzed, report both conditional and unconditional curves and model the selection event.
A claimed circuit should specify score matrix, normalization, sign, tie breaking, and action readout precisely enough to reproduce predictions.
World-model terminology is most informative when paired with transition/reward prediction or a causal state intervention, not merely a decodable task variable.
Toy algorithmic tasks become stronger interpretability tests when they include held-out lengths, vocabulary permutations, causal ablations, and alternative-policy baselines.
Negative cells and failed seeds are mechanistic evidence rather than nuisance runs; they can distinguish representation failure from readout or optimization failure.
open_questions: Does the width effect persist at fixed total parameter count or when only Q/K rank is varied while token/value/readout capacity is held constant?
Are the analyzed values raw attention logits or post-softmax weights, and does the result hold for both?
Can activation patching, rank-direction ablation, or counterfactual edits causally change predicted swaps as the proposed mechanism requires?
What exact signed gap statistic and tie rule maximizes out-of-sample action prediction, and what explains the remaining top-2 mismatches?
Do policies trained at length 6 generalize to 7 or 8, and do the same attention and gap metrics predict that transfer?
Does the scalar order code survive a random relabeling of token identities, repeated values, unseen values, or removal of learned positional embeddings?
How do successful and failed agents differ over training time before conditioning on terminal accuracy?
Would a simple MLP, RNN, supervised transformer, or hand-coded adjacent-inversion policy exhibit the same or cleaner internal rank code?
Can the value matrix and actor head be algebraically decomposed to show an actual adjacent-difference computation?
What constitutes a world model in this environment, and can the agent predict transitions or plan under partial observability?
Why is the length-6 10M mean below the 1M mean, and how were widths and seeds allocated across Table 1's training budgets?
Does higher width improve robustness under pruning, quantization, input noise, or adversarial permutations, as speculated?

competitive_landscape.title: Learning Transformer Programs
competitive_landscape.difference: Friedman et al. train modified transformers on sorting and other algorithmic tasks and automatically compile them into discrete human-readable Python programs, providing a more complete executable account than attention correlations. The target uses an ordinary minimal PPO transformer and asks how width affects an emergent heuristic, but it does not compare with this directly relevant interpretable-sorting approach.

competitive_landscape.title: Emergent Linear Representations in World Models of Self-Supervised Sequence Models
competitive_landscape.difference: Nanda et al. recover a linear Othello board representation and use vector interventions to control behavior, supporting a causal link between state code and output. The target finds a simpler scalar permutation-rank correlation in a shallower RL policy but performs no intervention, so its world-model evidence is weaker despite a broader seed/width sweep.

competitive_landscape.title: Emergent World Representations: Exploring a Sequence Model Trained on a Synthetic Task
competitive_landscape.difference: Li et al. uncover an internal Othello board representation and intervene to alter legal-move predictions, operationalizing a hidden dynamic state. The target's sorting state is directly observed and its attention rank code is not causally manipulated, though the controlled width sweep adds a capacity axis absent from Othello-GPT.

competitive_landscape.title: A Toy Model of Universality: Reverse Engineering how Networks Learn Group Operations
competitive_landscape.difference: Chughtai et al. characterize full families of circuits across groups and architectures and show that precise circuits and their learning order vary between networks. The target likewise studies many toy-task agents but proposes one partial attention/gap pattern without an equivalent circuit taxonomy or weight-level reverse engineering.
competitive_landscape.source_version: PMLR volume 202, ICML 2023 proceedings edition, pp. 6243-6267

competitive_landscape.title: Can Transformers Learn to Solve Problems Recursively?
competitive_landscape.difference: Zhang et al. reconstruct shortcut algorithms for structurally recursive functions and use them to predict 91% of failures, emphasizing out-of-distribution limits. The target examines adjacent sorting and width but neither tests longer inputs nor validates whether its hypothesized heuristic predicts individual failures comparably well.

competitive_landscape.title: SortBench: Benchmarking LLMs based on their ability to sort lists
competitive_landscape.difference: SortBench varies list difficulty and surfaces faithfulness, syntax-versus-semantics, long-list, and overthinking failures in deployed LLMs. The target provides deeper internal access to tiny trained agents, but tests only distinct fixed tokens at lengths 6/8 and therefore omits the robustness regimes that make SortBench challenging.

competitive_landscape.title: Transformers Linearly Represent Highly Structured World Models
competitive_landscape.difference: Kniazev and Fijalkow analyze an 8-layer Sudoku trace model, identify constraint-substructure state geometry, and recover sparse monosemantic naked-single neurons that promote specific outputs. This subsequent work supplies a richer state and end-to-end circuit account; the target remains distinctive for quantitatively linking width to representational cleanliness across hundreds of RL runs.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The authors claim a quantitative demonstration that larger embedding dimensions create a stronger, more faithful, consistent, and robust transformer world model after task performance saturates, with a global-order attention representation and largest-adjacent-difference action circuit recurring across hundreds of PPO agents.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The paper contributes a compact adjacent-swap RL testbed, exhaustive same-length action evaluation, a 475-agent width sweep, normalized order and action-gap metrics, and selected attention visualizations. Earlier work already studies sorting transformers, toy-task circuit families, Othello world states with causal interventions, recursive-algorithm shortcuts, and sorting robustness. No checked predecessor exactly combines PPO adjacent-swap sorting with an embedding-width sweep of these two internal statistics.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The narrow empirical observation—that successful wider versions of this particular minimal policy tend to exhibit cleaner final-row scalar rank codes and stronger gap/action association—appears novel. The broad claims do not follow: width is confounded with total capacity and optimization success; high-accuracy postselection is substantial at length 8; the gap rule is partial and underspecified; no causal circuit or robustness test is performed; and the model is not shown to predict world dynamics. This is best framed as a descriptive toy-model capacity study and hypothesis generator, not evidence that model size generally strengthens world models or interpretability.

reviewer_notes: Primary full-text pass completed against every physical page of the pinned 14-page arXiv:2510.18315v2 preprint, including all formulas, Tables 1-3, Figures 1-8, references, and Appendix A. The official arXiv record was checked on 2026-08-23 and identifies v2, revised 2026-07-14, as current; the pinned PDF bytes and extracted text match the provenance hashes above. Seven exact-current official competitors were checked. The missing softmax was confirmed visually in the PDF equation, not inferred from text extraction. The adjacent-swap failure claim was audited against the exact inversion-count property: any adjacent inversion swap decreases the minimum remaining swap count by one, so the described need to temporarily worsen local inversions is false. Confidence is high in the numerical/table transcription and mathematical audits, moderate-high in the confounding assessment, and lower for any statement about the unpublished implementation because the paper omits a complete agent-allocation table and artifact URL.
